title: Work and Power in Electrical Circuits
topicTitle: Work and power in electrical circuits
notes: **Electrical work:** $W = VIt = I^2Rt = V^2t/R$. Work done by a current is the energy transferred.
**Electrical power:** $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$. Power is the rate of energy transfer.
**Joule heating:** $P = I^2R$ is the power dissipated as heat in a resistor. This is also called $I^2R$ loss.
**Kilowatt-hour:** unit of electrical energy. $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6\\\\,\	ext{J}$. This is what electricity meters measure.
**Efficiency:** useful power output divided by total power input. Transmission lines use high voltage to reduce $I^2R$ losses because $P_{loss} \\\\propto I^2$.

**Power in different elements:** in a resistor, all electrical energy is converted to heat: $P = I^2R$. In a motor, electrical energy converts to mechanical work plus heat: $P_{input} = VI = I^2R + P_{mech}$. In a battery being charged, electrical energy is stored as chemical energy: $P_{input} = \\\\mathcal{E}I + I^2r$.

**Energy conservation in circuits:** the total electrical energy supplied equals the sum of energy dissipated as heat and energy converted to other forms: $V_{source} \\\\cdot I \\\\cdot t = I^2Rt + \	ext{other forms}$.
**Power rating of resistors:** resistors are rated by the maximum power they can dissipate without damage. Common ratings are 0.25 W, 0.5 W, and 1 W. Exceeding this causes overheating and failure.
**Domestic electrical cost:** the cost of running an appliance is $\	ext{Cost} = P(\	ext{kW}) \	imes t(\	ext{h}) \	imes \	ext{rate (per kWh)}$. A 100 W bulb running for 5 hours uses 0.5 kWh.
**Power factor:** for AC circuits, $P = VI\\\\cos\\\\phi$, where $\\\\cos\\\\phi$ is the power factor. For DC circuits, $\\\\cos\\\\phi = 1$, so $P = VI$ always.
**Heat energy in calories:** $H = 0.24 I^2 R t$ calories (mechanical equivalent of heat). In SI units, $H = I^2 R t$ joules.
confusion: Power $P = I^2R$ and $P = V^2/R$ are both correct but apply in different contexts. Use $I^2R$ when current is known (series circuits). Use $V^2/R$ when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Using the wrong one gives a wrong answer because $V$ and $I$ are not independent.
Electrical energy is measured in joules (J) or kilowatt-hours (kWh), NOT in watts (W). Watt is a unit of power (energy per time). $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 100 W bulb connected to 230 V draws less current than a 60 W bulb (because $I = P/V$, so the 100 W bulb has $I = 0.43$ A vs $I = 0.26$ A for the 60 W bulb). The 100 W bulb actually has LOWER resistance.

In a series circuit, the higher-wattage bulb glows dimmer because it has lower resistance, and in series the same current flows through both: $P = I^2R$, so the higher resistance (60 W bulb) gets more power.
Power dissipated in internal resistance ($I^2r$) is wasted energy. This is why battery-powered devices get warm - the internal resistance converts some chemical energy to heat instead of useful work.
practice: A 60 W, 230 V bulb is connected to a 230 V supply. Find the current, resistance, and energy consumed in 5 hours. Solution: $I = P/V = 60/230 = 0.261$ A. $R = V/I = 230/0.261 = 881\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $W = Pt = 60 \	imes 5 = 300\\\\,\	ext{Wh} = 0.3\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 1.08 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 12 V car headlamp draws 5 A. Find the power, resistance, and cost of running it for 4 hours at 8 pence per kWh. Solution: $P = VI = 12 \	imes 5 = 60$ W. $R = V/I = 12/5 = 2.4\\\\,\\\\Omega$. Energy $= 60 \	imes 4/1000 = 0.24\\\\,\	ext{kWh}$. Cost $= 0.24 \	imes 8 = 1.92$ pence.

A 100 $\\\Omega$ resistor carries a current of 2 A for 5 minutes. Find the heat produced in joules and calories. Solution: $H = I^2Rt = 4 \	imes 100 \	imes 300 = 120000$ J. In calories: $H = 120000/4.184 = 28681$ cal $\\\\approx 28.7$ kcal.

A transmission line carries 100 A at 11 kV over a total resistance of 5 $\\\Omega$. Find the power loss and the percentage of power lost. Solution: $P_{loss} = I^2R = 10000 \	imes 5 = 50000$ W $= 50$ kW. Power transmitted $= VI = 11000 \	imes 100 = 1.1 \	imes 10^6$ W $= 1100$ kW. Percentage loss $= 50/1100 = 4.5\\\\%$.

A 1.5 V cell with internal resistance 0.5 $\\\Omega$ is connected to a variable resistor. Find the resistance for maximum power transfer and the power delivered. Solution: $R = r = 0.5\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 1.5/(0.5+0.5) = 1.5$ A. $P_{max} = I^2R = 2.25 \	imes 0.5 = 1.125$ W.
universalFacts: A 100 W incandescent bulb is only about 5% efficient - most electrical energy is converted to heat rather than visible light. LEDs are about 15-20% efficient but produce far more lumens per watt.

Electric transmission lines carry power at very high voltages (up to 765 kV) to minimize $I^2R$ losses. Halving the voltage doubles the current and quadruples the power loss, which is why high-voltage transmission is essential.
The unit of electrical energy consumption, the kilowatt-hour, is not an SI unit. The SI unit of energy is the joule: $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.
A typical household circuit breaker is rated for 15-20 A at 120-240 V, giving a maximum power of 1.8-4.8 kW. Connecting too many high-power appliances can trip the breaker or cause a fire.
The heating effect of current was discovered by James Prescott Joule in 1841. His law $H = I^2Rt$ is a fundamental result of energy conservation in electrical circuits.
summary: The work done by a current in a circuit is the electrical energy it transfers, and it can be written in four equivalent forms: W = VIt = I²Rt = V²t/R, all of which agree because Ohm's law relates V, I and R. The corresponding power, that is the rate of energy transfer, is likewise P = VI = I²R = V²/R. In a resistor all of this electrical energy appears as heat, the Joule heating P = I²R, and the same expression is called the I²R loss when describing energy wasted in transmission lines. Because that loss grows with the square of the current, power is transmitted at high voltage and low current, which is why grid systems step the voltage up for transmission and step it down near the user. Energy itself is measured in joules or in kilowatt-hours, with 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, and it is the kilowatt-hour that domestic electricity meters record, since the watt is a unit of power. In devices that are not pure resistors the input power VI splits into useful output plus heating, so a motor obeys P_input = VI = I²R + P_mech while a cell being charged stores part of its input as chemical energy.
importantConcepts: Electrical work in four equivalent forms, W = VIt = I²Rt = V²t/R, all equivalent through Ohm's law.
Electrical power as the rate of energy transfer, P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
Joule heating P = I²R, the power dissipated as heat in a resistor, also called the I²R loss.
The kilowatt-hour as the practical unit of electrical energy, 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, recorded by domestic meters.
Transmission at high voltage and low current to reduce I²R losses, which grow with the square of the current.
Power splitting in non-resistive devices, so that a motor obeys P_input = VI = I²R + P_mech and a charging cell stores part of its input chemically.
importantStatements: The work done by a current in time t is W = VIt = I²Rt = V²t/R.
The power dissipated as heat in a resistor is P = I²R.
One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules, and it is energy that is measured in kilowatt-hours, not power in watts.
Since transmission loss P = I²R grows as the square of the current, high-voltage low-current transmission is used to reduce losses.
In any steady circuit the total electrical energy supplied equals the sum of the energy dissipated as heat and the energy converted into other forms.
importantTasks: Calculate the current, resistance and energy consumed by a rated appliance such as a bulb from its power and voltage rating.
Choose between the forms P = I²R and P = V²/R according to whether the current or the voltage across the component is known.
Convert an energy reading in kilowatt-hours into joules, and a power in watts into kilowatts.
Write an energy balance for a circuit or a device in which part of the input power is dissipated as heat and part is converted into useful output.
keyPoints: Pick the power form to match what is given: I²R when the current is known, V²/R when the voltage across the component is known.
Watts are power and joules are energy, so a 60 W bulb running for 5 h uses 300 Wh = 0.3 kWh, not 300 W.
The I² dependence of transmission loss is the whole reason for the national grid using very high voltages.
For a series circuit the same current flows through every component, so I²R is the convenient form; in a parallel circuit the same voltage applies, so V²/R is.
Joule heating converts electrical energy irreversibly into thermal energy, which is why resistors warm up in use.
specialNotes: P = I²R and P = V²/R are both correct but suit different data: use I²R where the current is known, as in a series circuit, and V²/R where the voltage is known, as in a parallel circuit.
Energy is measured in joules or kilowatt-hours and never in watts, since the watt is a unit of power, that is energy per unit time; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
The I² factor means halving the current reduces the resistive loss to a quarter, which is exactly why transmission voltage is stepped up and the current stepped down.
In a pure resistor all the input power leaves as heat, so P = I²R is both the useful output and the unavoidable loss.
For a motor or a charging cell the input power VI splits into heating and useful output, so equating VI with I²R alone understates the output.
examShortTricks: Select the form of the power formula to match the data: I²R for a known current, V²/R for a known voltage, VI for a known pair.
For a rated appliance, P = VI gives the current directly and R = V/I follows, which settles most household-appliance numericals in two lines.
Convert energy with 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J and remember that the kilowatt-hour is what a meter displays, so read the number and attach the unit.
In a series circuit the current is common to every component, so I²R gives the power in each one directly.
examNotes: A three mark numerical on a household appliance, finding the current, the resistance and the energy used in a stated time, is very common.
One mark questions ask for the SI unit of power, the unit of energy and the value of 1 kWh in joules.
Transmission-loss questions appear regularly and are answered by pointing out that P_loss = I²R varies as the square of the current.
Expect a five mark energy balance in which the supplied energy is shared between heat and useful output in a motor or a cell.
